\section{Discussion and Conclusion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Granger precedence is not causation.}
Granger causality tests predictive improvement, not true causation~\cite{granger1969investigating,shojaie2022granger}: an unobserved process could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics.
Our central claim is scoped accordingly---``token entropy Granger-precedes diversity collapse''---and bivariate tests cannot exclude confounders; multivariate VAR models would be required for confounder testing.

\paragraph{Practical utility paradox.}
The framework works best where it is least needed: at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, PermG reliably detects canary precedence, but degradation is already severe; at $\alpha{\leq}0.45$, detection remains null.
In realistic pipelines where contamination increases over time, a continuous monitoring dashboard would trigger when $\alpha$ crosses the detectability threshold; the regime map itself is actionable output.

\paragraph{Four-layer detection taxonomy.}
Our results suggest a layered taxonomy: (1)~distributional dimensionality (effective rank, onset $\alpha{\approx}0.10$); (2)~distributional instability (entropy variance, suggestive at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$); (3)~causal coupling (Granger-type, onset $\alpha_c{\approx}0.50$); (4)~dynamical stability (AC1, suggestive at $T{=}11$).
The 40-percentage-point gap between Layers~1 and~3 constitutes the detection phase transition; Layers~2 and~4 require longer generation protocols ($T{\geq}50$; \citealt{dakos2012methods}).
Exploratory analysis reveals a CSD-consistent pattern---canary metrics show rising autocorrelation (Kendall $\tau{=}0.79$--$0.82$) while downstream metrics show none---but this does not survive multiple testing correction (2/10 post-BH).

\paragraph{Method recommendation.}
The multi-method comparison converges on PermG as the recommended method: zero null-control FPR, consistent detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$, and clean directional separation (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse at $\alpha{=}1.0$ on WikiText).
The remaining four methods each exhibit characteristic limitations detailed in \S\ref{sec:method}.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
Lead-lag analysis in iterative training collapse is far more fragile than assumed: method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to 75\% null-control FPR, first-differencing exposes canary$\to$perplexity associations as entirely spurious, and regime dependence causes the same test to shift from significant to null.
PermG identifies token entropy as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse, validated across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) with detection in 13 cases (87\%).
Directional asymmetry is domain-dependent: unidirectional on WikiText across all regimes, while C4 exhibits seed-sensitive bidirectional coupling (s42: 7/8 reverse vs.\ s43: 1/8; preliminary).
SmolLM3-3B reveals architecture-dependent canary sensitivity (ECE-only detection, 3/8; \S\ref{sec:generalization}); bf16 precision effects at $\alpha{=}0.60$ require fp32 confirmation.
Canary-based predictive cessation reduces peak perplexity by 58\%.
Extended discussion appears in Appendix~\ref{app:extended_discussion}.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Model collapse and canary metrics.}
Iterative training collapse was formalized by \citet{shumailov2024curse} and \citet{alemohammad2024mad}, who showed that recursively replacing real data with model-generated text causes progressive tail erosion.
Theoretical analyses have sharpened these results: \citet{dohmatob2024tale} recast collapse as a change in scaling-law exponents, and \citet{dohmatob2025strong} proved that collapse can occur even when synthetic data constitutes a vanishingly small fraction of the training set.
Several works have since proposed monitoring metrics: \citet{du2026geometric} observe that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades; \citet{du2025scales} report ECE increases of 75\% at 30\% synthetic contamination before accuracy drops; and \citet{gambetta2024surplexity} introduces surplexity as a simultaneous collapse detector and data filter.
Other approaches track spectral divergence~\cite{sigma2026spectral}, topological features~\cite{kalinowski2026topology}, or center-edge sampling dynamics~\cite{dces2026counter}.
We differ from the closest predecessor, \citet{du2026geometric}, in four respects: (i)~we compare an entire family of canary metrics rather than a single pair; (ii)~we cross-validate across five independent statistical methods with inter-method sensitivity quantification; (iii)~we map detectability as a function of contamination regime; and (iv)~we treat method-selection sensitivity itself as a primary finding.

\paragraph{Early-warning signals and lead-lag methodology.}
The theoretical foundation for canary-based prediction originates in ecology: \citet{scheffer2009early} established that systems approaching tipping points exhibit generic early-warning signals, while \citet{boettiger2012limits} quantified detection limits in short time series---a constraint directly relevant to iterative training, where generation counts ($T{=}5$--$20$) are far smaller than typical ecological datasets.
\citet{gu2025datamixing} show that data mixing can induce phase transitions in knowledge acquisition, providing a direct theoretical analogue to the detection phase transition we observe: a critical mixing ratio separates qualitatively different regimes.
The non-monotonic dose-response we find parallels hormetic patterns in toxicology~\cite{calabrese2003hormesis}, where low-dose stimulation and high-dose inhibition produce U-shaped curves.
The standard econometric framework for testing temporal precedence is Granger causality~\cite{granger1969investigating}; however, standard Granger tests applied to non-stationary series produce inflated rejection rates~\cite{granger1974spurious}, and the Toda--Yamamoto procedure~\cite{toda1995statistical} addresses this at the cost of reduced degrees of freedom severe in short series.
These methods are largely absent from the model collapse literature, which relies on visual inspection or naive cross-correlation.

\paragraph{Analytical robustness.}
The broader issue of researcher degrees of freedom in ML has received increasing attention: \citet{bell2022modeling} introduced multiverse analysis, \citet{coretta2023multidimensional} demonstrated that 46 independent teams reached substantially different conclusions on identical data, and \citet{kapoor2024reforms} synthesized these concerns into a consensus checklist.
Our work applies this multiverse perspective to model collapse: five statistical methods across multiple contamination regimes produce conclusions ranging from universal significance to complete null on the same dataset.
No prior work bridges the collapse monitoring and econometric lead-lag literatures with systematic multi-method cross-validation, differencing diagnostics, false discovery correction, and regime-dependent calibration.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Our experiments are validated at scales ${\leq}6.9$B parameters across six decoder-only transformer families; whether the temporal lead persists at frontier scale is open.
Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 and C4 subsets, three orders of magnitude smaller than production corpora; C4 results carry a pre-training data confound (Pythia was pre-trained on Pile, which overlaps with C4).
With $T{=}10$ (11 data points), threshold onset and Toda--Yamamoto are power-limited; $T{\geq}20$ validation is pending.
PermG requires null-control ($\alpha{=}0.0$) calibration data, which may not be available in all deployment settings.
The $\alpha{=}0.60$ results use bf16 precision from a single seed; fp32 multi-seed confirmation is needed.
Canary claims are scoped to distinct-$n$ diversity~\cite{li2016diversity}, not model collapse broadly~\cite{schaeffer2025position}; replace-only protocol means accumulate-mode dynamics~\cite{dey2024breaking} are untested.
